title: An ADHD Cleaning Routine for When You Have Zero Energy
description: A realistic ADHD cleaning routine built for low-energy days: 3 tiny levels, 15-minute blocks and no guilt. Clean enough is the goal.
intro:
Most cleaning routines are written by people whose brains send them a helpful little memo that says "time to wipe the counters." Ours send a memo too. It says "what if we reorganized the entire garage at 11pm instead."

So let's skip the color-coded daily schedule you'll abandon by Thursday. This routine is built for the days you have *nothing* in the tank, and it scales up on the days you do.

The goal isn't a clean house. The goal is a house that's clean *enough* to function, and a routine you can pick back up after a bad week without starting over.

sections.heading: The three levels
sections.body:
Every day you pick one level. Not the level you think you should do. The level you actually have energy for today.

- **Level 1 — Survival (5 minutes):** Dishes that you need tomorrow, trash out, one surface cleared.
- **Level 2 — Maintenance (15 minutes):** Level 1 plus a quick pick-up of the main room and a wipe of the kitchen counters.
- **Level 3 — Bonus (30 minutes):** Level 2 plus one "real" task: bathroom, floors or laundry.

Level 1 counts as a win. Write that on a sticky note if you need to. Doing Level 1 on a hard day keeps the house from sliding, and that is the whole game.

sections.heading: Why tiny levels work for our brains
sections.body:
When a task feels huge, our brains refuse to start. Starting is the hard part, not the doing. A five-minute level is small enough that the refusal doesn't kick in.

And here's the sneaky part: once you start, you'll often keep going. Momentum is real. But you're never *required* to keep going. Permission to stop is exactly what makes starting possible.

sections.heading: Set up your 'reset kit' once
sections.body:
Low-energy cleaning fails when you have to go find things. Before your next good day, set up a caddy with:

- A multi-surface spray
- Two or three microfiber cloths
- A small trash bag
- A handheld vacuum or mini dustpan

Keep it somewhere central, not under the sink behind the dish soap. When it's grab-and-go, a five-minute clean is actually five minutes, not five minutes of searching plus five of cleaning.

sections.heading: The 15-minute block, step by step
sections.body:
On a Level 2 day, set a timer for 15 minutes and go in this order:

1. **Trash first.** Walk through with a bag and grab anything that's obviously trash. Instant visual win.
2. **Dishes to the kitchen.** Every cup and plate goes to the sink area. Don't wash yet.
3. **Things with a home go home.** Only stuff where you know the spot without thinking.
4. **Wipe one surface.** Kitchen counter or bathroom sink. Pick one.
5. **Stop when the timer goes.** Seriously. Stopping on time teaches your brain the timer can be trusted.

Things that don't have a home go into one basket. You'll deal with that basket on a Level 3 day, not now.

sections.heading: Make it easier to start
sections.body:
A few tricks that help the routine actually happen:

- **Stack it onto something you already do.** Level 1 happens while the coffee brews or the kettle boils.
- **Put on a specific playlist.** Three songs is about 10 minutes. Your brain learns the cue.
- **Body double.** Call a friend, or put on a "clean with me" video. Someone else moving makes you want to move.
- **Lower the bar out loud.** Say "I'm only doing trash." Weirdly, saying it makes it easier.

sections.heading: When you miss days (you will)
sections.body:
Missing days isn't failing the routine. It's part of the routine. On the first day back, do Level 1 only, even if the house is wrecked. Especially if the house is wrecked.

Then Level 1 again tomorrow. By day three or four, you'll usually have the energy for a Level 2. The routine bends so it doesn't break.

finds.name: Cleaning caddy with handle
finds.why: Everything goes room to room with you, so you're not walking back and forth mid-task.

finds.name: Cordless handheld vacuum
finds.why: Grab, zap, done. No cord and no big vacuum means small messes get handled right away.

finds.name: Visual countdown timer
finds.search: visual countdown timer for kids and adults
finds.why: A shrinking color disk shows how much time is left, so "a few minutes" becomes real.

outro:
Pick your level today. Do it. Count it. That's the routine.

If you like having it on paper, our *Tidy Brain Printable Pack* has the three levels as a checklist you can stick on the fridge and tick off, plus a "clean enough" weekly reset page.
